extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; natural philosophers, experimental scientists, physicians and chemists reading Philosophical Transactions
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and interpreting experimental observations and demonstrations in natural philosophy (meteorology, fluid mechanics, chemistry, and clinical case histories), including methods, data tables, causal arguments, and conceptual clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical examination procedure and interpretive criteria for human calculi
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests of calculi by application of reagents and distillation to determine solubility and constituent parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply acids and reagents and record reactions: pouring spirit of sulphur, vitriol (sulphuric acid), acetic produced some effervescence in loose/friable calculi but no solution; spirit of sal ammoniac had no action; nitric acid (sp. nitri acidus) dissolved them completely. Distillation of calculi yields volatile salt, volatile spirit, water (phlegma), much 'earth' and little fixed salt (variation depending on origin — stomach vs intestines/bladder). Adding spirit of vitriol to distilled liquor turns it red then turbid with deposition; pouring vitriol on caput mortuum or lixiviated salt produced violent effervescence. From these reactions conclude constituent proportions (e.g., large proportion earth, small volatile salt, little acid, modified by urinous salts/spirit). Record weights/yields (example: 6 oz yielded 5 oz 2 dr caput mortuum, etc.) and distillation residues to support composition inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting medical case histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a detailed chronological account of symptoms, treatments, observed events, and outcomes for clinical cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dates and sequence (e.g., onset, transient improvements, relapses), symptoms (nausea, hiccup, pains, convulsions, haemorrhage), treatments used (cordial medicine, dulcified spirit of nitre, bleeding, clysters), objective expulsions/findings (voided calculi with size/appearance, gangrene, angina, hemorrhage), patterns over time (frequency of stone passage), associated observations (urine volume, consistency, vomiting of urine-like fluid), and follow-up status. Where possible include illustrations/figures of specimens and pursue chemical/analytical follow-up; terminate the history with clear statement of what remains to be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for computing altitude from barometer readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine height of a place (altitude) or the expected barometer mercury height using the reciprocal relation between air expansion and mercury height together with geometrical/logarithmic methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model air expansion as reciprocally proportional to mercury height and use the hyperbola/its asymptotes so that areas under the hyperbola correspond to sums of infinitesimal expansions; apply Gregory of St. Vincent's demonstration equating such areas to logarithms. Use standard reference values (e.g., barometer ~30 in, air specific gravity ~1:800 relative to water, mercury to water ~13.6:1) to build tables converting inches of mercury to feet of altitude and vice versa. Note assumptions (uniform air properties) and produce tables for practical use (example tables given mapping inches to feet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical correlations between barometer behavior and weather/wind
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed regularities linking barometer (mercury) height/variation with weather conditions and wind patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the following empirical observations as interpretation rules: (1) In calm weather when air inclined to rain the mercury is commonly low; (2) In serene, settled weather the mercury is generally high; (3) On very great winds (even without rain) the mercury sinks lowest relative to the wind direction; (4) Ceteris paribus, highest mercury readings are found with easterly and north-easterly winds (in the author’s locality); (5) In calm frosty weather the mercury generally stands high; (6) After very great storms when mercury has been low it generally rises very fast; (7) More northerly places show greater barometer alterations than more southerly; (8) Within/toward the tropics there is very little variation of mercury height (except on hurricanes). Use these as interpretive heuristics but check local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal hypothesis for barometer rise and fall (variable winds and vapour content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain barometer changes primarily by variations in the amount/motion of air (variable winds) and secondarily by changing vapour content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat variable winds as the principal cause: opposing winds can evacuate or accumulate air over a place, thus diminishing or increasing the incumbent cylinder of air and lowering/rising the mercury. Consider vapour rise/fall (vapours lodging or being dissipated) as a secondary effect that alters air crowding and weight. Apply these causal mechanisms to explain the empirical correlations listed and to predict short-term changes (e.g., rapid post-storm rise from recoil/accession of new air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of assumptions and confounders in barometric methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limitations of the simple barometer–altitude and barometer–weather models and compensate for variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the atmosphere is a single unaltered body of constant specific gravity: account for temporal changes in total atmospheric weight (observed barometer variations), thermal expansion/contraction due to heat/cold, and admixture of heavier effluvia/vapours. Recognize that rarefaction/condensation may deviate from the ideal reciprocal law at extremes and that local composition and temperature effects may compensate or offset each other in practice. Explicitly state these limits when presenting calculations or interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental rules for jets and spouting waters (design and measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical and experimental relations governing height and quantity of jets and flows from reservoirs and bores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key rules to use/design/measure jets: (a) Quantity expelled by jets of the same bore at different reservoir heights varies in the subduplicate proportion (i.e., proportional to square root) of those heights; (b) Quantity evacuated by different bores at the same height is proportional to the squares of their diameters; (c) Jets never rise as high as their reservoirs but fall short by amounts in duplicate proportion to the heights they rise to; (d) An even polished round hole at the pipe end gives a higher jet than cylindrical or conical ajutages (though conical is the better of those two). Use experiments to verify and to choose ajutages in engineering applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium of fluids and rules for floating bodies and jet forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply mechanics principles to demonstrate how fluids counterpoise weight and to derive forces of jets and behaviour of floating bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive rules from mechanical principles: show how fluids counterbalance each other's weight, how elasticity (spring) of air and flame is counterpoised by weight, and how to compute the force of jets from reservoir height and pipe geometry. Use these derivations to produce engineering rules (e.g., for wind/water mill comparative force) and to compute expected jet amplitudes and ranges as per Galileo/Torricelli doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental derivation of the origin of fountains and water budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measurement and experiment to argue the origin of springs/fountains from rain infiltration and to estimate sufficiency for river discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect precipitation and discharge measurements to show rain falling in catchment areas can supply rivers (example: in countries near Seine fountains, at least seven times as much rain falls as the river discharges). Trace percolation paths until encountering impermeable layers and use experiments/measurements to infer fountains' origins. Present quantitative experiments on flow through bores to substantiate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue of causes of winds (general and particular) as explanatory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate and use multiple causes (general and particular) to explain wind origins and variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a plural causal framework: general causes include (1) diurnal motion of the earth, (2) condensation/rarefaction of the air caused by solar heat, and (3) lunar distance effects (apogee/perigee). Particular causes include extraordinary rising of vapours/exhalations from local places, heavy rains/hails, nitrous/sulphureous exhalations associated with earthquakes, and sudden melting of mountain snow. Use these causes to interpret local wind phenomena rather than a single-factor explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual and rhetorical standards in natural-philosophical argument (Boyle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague appeals to 'nature' — substitute precise concepts, distinguish kinds of 'nature', and critically examine received axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing/arguing in natural philosophy: do not rely on the vulgar, ambiguous notion of 'nature'; instead substitute clearer terms and distinctions (e.g., 'cosmical mechanism' for general nature and 'individual mechanism' for particular nature). Explicitly state reasons for rejecting received notions and axioms, address common objections, and treat widely accepted aphorisms (natura vacuum horret; natura est morborum medicatrix) with rigorous analysis. Aim for conceptual precision and be willing to recede from common opinion when warranted by argument/experiment.
